questions.stem: A 32-year-old man develops crampy abdominal pain and watery diarrhea two days after eating undercooked food at a picnic. Stool culture grows a bacterial pathogen. Which of the following is the most likely portal of entry for this organism?

explanation.summary: Most gastrointestinal pathogens enter through ingestion of food or water contaminated with fecal matter.
explanation.whyCorrect: The GI tract is a common portal of entry when its defenses (gastric acid, peristalsis, IgA, and normal microbiota) are overcome. Food or water contaminated by feces delivers the organism, and abdominal pain with diarrhea points to a gut infection acquired by the fecal-oral route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhalation delivers respiratory pathogens to the airways, not organisms causing diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Broken skin is a portal for wound and catheter-associated infections, not enteric disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The urethra is the entry point for urinary tract, not gastrointestinal, pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde neuronal transport is how certain viruses reach the CNS, not how gut bacteria are acquired.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A physiologist studies how the upper airway resists infection. She observes that inhaled particles are trapped in a sticky mucus layer and swept by hair-like projections toward the throat, where they are cleared. Which of the following defense mechanisms is being described?

explanation.summary: The respiratory tract relies on mucociliary clearance to trap and remove inhaled microbes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucus traps large particles while cilia beat them toward the back of the throat for clearance; only small particles reach the alveoli, where immune cells phagocytose them. This trapping-and-sweeping description defines mucociliary clearance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric acidity is a gastrointestinal defense that kills ingested organisms in the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peristalsis is the wave-like movement of the GI tract that prevents microbial overgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urinary flushing is a urogenital defense that clears organisms from the urethra.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antimicrobial fatty acids are a defense of the skin surface, not the airway.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and then develops profuse watery diarrhea. Colonoscopy reveals adherent yellow-white plaques on the colonic mucosa, and toxin testing is positive. Which of the following best explains her increased susceptibility to this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disruption of the normal gut microbiota

choices.label: E
choices.text: Breakdown of the keratinized epidermal barrier

explanation.summary: Antibiotics disrupt the protective gut microbiota, allowing C. difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The normal gut microbiota competes with arriving organisms and limits their colonization. Antibiotics kill this resident flora, letting C. difficile proliferate and release toxins A and B, which produce the inflammatory pseudomembrane seen on the mucosa.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gastric acid protects against ingested organisms but is not the defense lost with antibiotic use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary clearance is a respiratory defense, unrelated to colonic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urine flow is a urogenital defense and has no role in colonic colonization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The epidermal barrier guards the skin, not the gut lumen where this infection occurs.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A neonate develops purulent conjunctivitis three days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The mother had an untreated sexually transmitted infection. Which of the following best describes how the pathogen was transmitted to the infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exposure during passage through the birth canal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding from a distant maternal focus

explanation.summary: Some pathogens are transmitted vertically as the infant passes through the birth canal.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exposure during passage through the birth canal transmits organisms such as Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, leading to neonatal conjunctivitis. The timing right after vaginal delivery and the maternal genital infection point to this route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Transplacental spread in utero characterizes TORCH agents and would cause congenital disease present at birth, not acquired during delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Breast milk transmits certain viruses (e.g., CMV, HIV, HBV) postnatally, not this early bacterial conjunctivitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory droplet inhalation is a person-to-person route unrelated to this genital pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hematogenous seeding describes spread within a host's bloodstream, not mother-to-infant transmission.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man who injects drugs intravenously presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Echocardiography shows friable vegetations on a heart valve, and blood cultures are positive. Which of the following best explains how the organism reached the heart valve?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct extension from an adjacent lung abscess

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis results from bloodborne spread of bacteria to the endocardium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous drug use introduces skin flora directly into the bloodstream, producing septicemia that seeds the endocardium. This hematogenous dissemination allows bacteria to form friable valvular vegetations, the hallmark of infective endocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Retrograde axonal transport carries certain viruses to the CNS, not bacteria to heart valves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal-oral ingestion is a portal for enteric infection, not for valve seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aspiration deposits organisms in the airway, not on the endocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no adjacent lung abscess described, and endocarditis is not typically produced by direct extension.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is bitten on the leg by a raccoon. Weeks later he develops difficulty swallowing, agitation, and a fatal encephalitis. By which of the following mechanisms did the causative virus most likely reach the central nervous system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lymphatic drainage to regional lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fecal-oral spread to the gastrointestinal tract

explanation.summary: Some viruses travel to the CNS by retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain viruses, including rabies, spread along nerves by retrograde axonal transport, moving from the bite site backward toward the central nervous system. The animal bite followed by fatal encephalitis is the classic presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematogenous spread uses the bloodstream and is not the route rabies takes to the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic drainage carries organisms to lymph nodes, not directly along nerves to the CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The virus is inoculated through the bite wound, not by extension across intact skin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fecal-oral spread delivers enteric pathogens to the gut, not neurotropic viruses to the brain.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic cough and night sweats undergoes lung biopsy, which shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells surrounding a central zone of caseous necrosis. Which of the following histologic patterns of reaction does this represent?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate without granulomas

explanation.summary: Epithelioid macrophages and giant cells around caseous necrosis define granulomatous inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatous inflammation features aggregates of activated (epithelioid) macrophages, often with giant cells; central caseating necrosis is characteristic of tuberculosis. The clinical picture of chronic cough and night sweats supports a mycobacterial granuloma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Suppurative inflammation is dominated by neutrophils and pus, not epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytopathic-cytoproliferative reactions are caused by viruses and show inclusion bodies, not caseating granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A diffuse lymphocytic infiltrate lacks the organized epithelioid macrophages and giant cells that define a granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bland scarring is end-stage fibrosis and does not include active giant cells or caseous necrosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with fever has a chest CT showing multiple lung lesions filled with pus. Biopsy of one lesion reveals a localized collection of neutrophils and necrotic debris consistent with an abscess. Which of the following types of organism most commonly produces this pattern of reaction?

explanation.summary: Suppurative inflammation with abscess formation is most commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Suppurative (purulent) inflammation is dominated by neutrophil infiltration, and pus is a collection of living and dying neutrophils and necrotic cells. Pyogenic bacteria are the classic cause, and an abscess is a localized collection of this pus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Viruses typically produce a cytopathic-cytoproliferative reaction, not neutrophil-rich abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes such as T. pallidum characteristically elicit a mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mycobacteria produce granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis rather than pus-filled abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inert foreign material triggers granulomatous, not suppurative, inflammation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: An immunosuppressed patient undergoes tissue biopsy that shows enlarged cells containing intranuclear inclusion bodies, with no neutrophils or granulomas present. This cytopathic pattern is most characteristic of infection by which of the following classes of pathogen?

explanation.summary: Inclusion bodies and cytopathic change without pus or granulomas point to a viral infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern is produced by viruses, which cause changes such as inclusion bodies and cell lysis; CMV is a classic example in immunosuppressed patients. The absence of neutrophils and granulomas argues against bacterial or mycobacterial causes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyogenic bacteria produce neutrophil-rich suppurative inflammation, not intranuclear inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycobacteria elicit granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid macrophages, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spirochetes cause a lymphocytic mononuclear infiltrate rather than viral inclusion bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Foreign material provokes a granulomatous foreign-body reaction, not cytopathic viral change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A patient with a gram-negative bloodstream infection becomes hypotensive with signs of shock. The responsible molecule is a component of the bacterial outer membrane whose lipid portion is detected by macrophages, triggering a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Which of the following is this molecule?

explanation.summary: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) is the gram-negative outer-membrane molecule that drives septic shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: LPS is an outer-membrane component of gram-negative bacteria whose Lipid A portion is detected by immune cells such as macrophages. This triggers pro-inflammatory and complement activation, and cytokine-induced hypotension can progress to shock.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphtheria toxin is a secreted A-B exotoxin of a gram-positive rod, not an outer-membrane lipid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exfoliative toxin is a Staphylococcus aureus protein that cleaves skin desmosomes, not an endotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxic shock syndrome toxin is a secreted superantigen protein, not a structural gram-negative membrane molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Staphylococcal enterotoxin is a preformed superantigen causing food poisoning, not a gram-negative outer-membrane component.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A child from an unvaccinated community develops a thick gray pseudomembrane over the pharynx and subsequently myocarditis. The responsible exotoxin is an A-B toxin. Which of the following best describes how its active subunit causes cell death?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of Lipid A to disrupt the membrane

explanation.summary: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin whose A subunit inhibits protein synthesis, causing cell death.
explanation.whyCorrect: In diphtheria, the B subunit binds and delivers the toxin into the host cell by endocytosis, and the A subunit then inhibits protein synthesis, leading to cell death. The toxin can enter the bloodstream and damage tissues such as myocardial cells, producing myocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 is the mechanism of the staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nonspecific massive cytokine release describes superantigens, not the diphtheria A-B toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipid A membrane effects belong to gram-negative endotoxin, not to this gram-positive exotoxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Degradation of secretory IgA is not the mechanism of diphtheria-toxin-mediated cell death.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops widespread superficial blistering and peeling of the skin. The causative Staphylococcus aureus toxin cleaves desmoglein-1, a protein that anchors keratinocytes together. Which of the following conditions results?

explanation.summary: Exfoliative toxin cleaving desmoglein-1 produces staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Exfoliative A and B toxins from S. aureus cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosomal protein, causing detachment of keratinocytes. The result is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, characterized by blistering and exfoliation that primarily affects pediatric patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic shock syndrome is caused by a superantigen and produces hypotension, not desmoglein-mediated skin peeling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudomembranous colitis is a C. difficile toxin-mediated colonic disease, unrelated to desmoglein-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphtheritic myocarditis results from diphtheria toxin inhibiting protein synthesis, not from cleaving skin proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Endotoxic shock is driven by gram-negative LPS, not by a staphylococcal skin toxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman reports several months of pain in her wrists, hands, elbows, and knees that improves with ibuprofen but never fully resolves. She has a red rash across both cheeks and the bridge of her nose, along with painful oral ulcers. Her temperature is 39.1 C (102.4 F). Laboratory studies show a decreased white blood cell count, hemoglobin, and platelet count. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A young woman with a malar (butterfly) rash, arthritis, oral ulcers, and pancytopenia has systemic lupus erythematosus.
explanation.whyCorrect: SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease that classically affects young women and presents with a butterfly-shaped malar rash, arthritis, oral/nasopharyngeal ulcers, and pancytopenia from autoantibodies that opsonize blood cells. Its features are summarized by the mnemonic RASH OR PAIN.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetric joint swelling of the hands and feet but does not produce a malar rash or pancytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goodpasture syndrome affects the lungs and kidneys with hemoptysis and glomerulonephritis, not a malar rash and arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis presents with sinus, lung, and kidney disease, not a malar rash with oral ulcers and arthralgias in this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a childhood disease with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and arthralgias.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a several-year history of systemic lupus erythematosus is evaluated with echocardiography. Imaging reveals small, single and multiple warty vegetations distributed on the surfaces of the mitral valve leaflets. Blood cultures are repeatedly negative. Which of the following best describes this cardiac finding?

explanation.summary: Sterile warty vegetations on the valve surface in a lupus patient are Libman-Sacks endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a nonbacterial verrucous endocarditis of SLE that produces small single or multiple warty deposits distinctively on the surface of the valve leaflets. Because it is immune-mediated rather than infectious, blood cultures are negative.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vegetations in infective endocarditis are considerably larger, contain infectious organisms, and would be associated with positive blood cultures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vegetations in rheumatic heart disease are smaller and are confined to the lines of closure of the leaflets, not scattered on the leaflet surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid nodules occur in subcutaneous tissue in rheumatoid arthritis, not as valvular vegetations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulomatous vasculitis is a feature of granulomatosis with polyangiitis affecting small vessels, not sterile valve vegetations.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a platelet count of 38,000/mm3 and scattered petechiae. Peripheral smear shows no schistocytes. Which of the following best explains the low platelet count in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies bind platelet glycoproteins, leading to splenic macrophage phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 causing platelet consumption in microthrombi

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibodies against the platelet basement membrane collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgA immune complexes depositing in the marrow

explanation.summary: Thrombocytopenia in SLE results from anti-platelet glycoprotein antibodies that mark platelets for splenic macrophage removal.
explanation.whyCorrect: In SLE, autoantibodies bind platelet membrane glycoproteins, leading to removal of the opsonized platelets by macrophages, particularly in the sinusoids of the spleen. This immune thrombocytopenia is the most common cytopenia mechanism described in lupus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with schistocytes, which are absent here and are not the lupus mechanism taught.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Marrow granulomas are not a described mechanism of the pancytopenia of SLE, which is antibody-mediated opsonization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-basement membrane collagen antibodies are the mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome, not lupus thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA immune complex deposition characterizes Henoch-Schonlein purpura, not SLE-related platelet destruction.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops pleuritic chest pain and glomerular injury. Her disease is understood to result from antigen-antibody complexes that deposit in tissues and activate complement, driving widespread inflammation. This process is an example of which of the following hypersensitivity reactions?

explanation.summary: SLE is a type III hypersensitivity reaction driven by immune-complex deposition and complement activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes SLE as due to a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which immune complexes deposit in tissue and activate complement, leading to widespread inflammation of the skin, serosa, kidney, and other organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I reactions are IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity such as anaphylaxis, not the immune-complex disease of lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type II reactions involve antibodies directed against fixed cell-surface antigens; SLE inflammation is attributed to circulating immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type IV reactions are delayed and T-cell mediated, whereas lupus tissue injury here is complement-activating immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type V receptor-stimulating hypersensitivity describes diseases like Graves disease, not lupus.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is being worked up for suspected systemic lupus erythematosus. An antinuclear antibody (ANA) test is positive. Which of the following additional antibodies is most specific for confirming the diagnosis of SLE?

explanation.summary: After a positive ANA, anti-dsDNA (or anti-Smith) antibodies help confirm systemic lupus erythematosus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ANA test is usually the initial screen, and if positive, sub-serologies are checked. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are specific for SLE and are used to confirm the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-CCP is specific for rheumatoid arthritis, found in about 70% of early cases, not for SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is the hallmark of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid factor is seen in rheumatoid arthritis and is nonspecific, appearing in other diseases as well.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with several months of symmetric swelling and morning stiffness of the small joints of her hands is suspected of having rheumatoid arthritis. Positivity for which of the following antibodies is most specific for this diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody for rheumatoid arthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-CCP antibodies are found in about 70% of patients with early rheumatoid arthritis and are highly specific for the disease, unlike rheumatoid factor which is nonspecific.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA is found in systemic lupus erythematosus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody is seen in Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA) is seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid factor is present in 75-80% of RA patients but is not specific because it appears in other diseases such as SLE.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has progressive destruction of the joints of her hands. Biopsy of an affected joint shows an expanding mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over and erodes the articular cartilage. Which of the following terms best describes this lesion?

explanation.summary: The proliferative synovial mass that erodes articular cartilage in RA is called a pannus.
explanation.whyCorrect: In rheumatoid arthritis, the inflamed synovium becomes edematous, thickened, and hyperplastic, forming a pannus, a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, granulation tissue, and fibroblasts that grows over and causes erosion of the articular cartilage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A rheumatoid nodule is a subcutaneous lesion with central fibrinoid necrosis and palisading macrophages, not the intra-articular mass eroding cartilage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A generic granuloma does not describe the specific proliferative synovial tissue of RA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A tophus is a deposit of urate crystals seen in gout, not rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A verrucous vegetation refers to the valvular lesions of Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has a firm subcutaneous nodule on the extensor surface of his forearm near the elbow. Biopsy shows a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a rim of activated macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A subcutaneous nodule with central fibrinoid necrosis rimmed by palisading macrophages in an RA patient is a rheumatoid nodule.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rheumatoid nodules are an infrequent manifestation of RA that occur in subcutaneous tissue of the forearm, elbow, occiput, and lumbosacral area. Microscopically they show a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a rim of activated macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A gouty tophus contains urate crystals, not a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis with palisading macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Libman-Sacks vegetations are sterile warty deposits on heart valves, not subcutaneous nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Goodpasture pulmonary lesion is intra-alveolar hemorrhage with hemosiderin-laden macrophages, not a subcutaneous nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Henoch-Schonlein lesions are palpable purpura from IgA immune complexes, not fibrinoid-necrosis nodules.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man presents with cough productive of blood and patchy consolidations on chest imaging, followed within weeks by hematuria and rising creatinine. Renal biopsy shows crescent formation in Bowman capsule with linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Autoantibodies in this patient are most likely directed against which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type IV collagen of the basement membrane

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by autoantibodies against type IV collagen in the basement membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Goodpasture syndrome occurs in the teens or twenties, more often in males, and is caused by circulating autoantibodies against type IV collagen found in the basement membrane. This produces linear IgG on the glomerular basement membrane, crescentic glomerulonephritis, and alveolar hemorrhage with hemoptysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are the marker of systemic lupus erythematosus, not Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) characterize granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies are specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-platelet glycoprotein antibodies cause the immune thrombocytopenia of SLE.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man is diagnosed with Goodpasture syndrome after presenting with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Which of the following treatments most directly targets the underlying cause of his disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Plasmapheresis to remove anti-basement membrane antibodies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron supplementation for chronic blood loss

explanation.summary: Goodpasture syndrome is treated with plasmapheresis to remove the pathogenic anti-basement membrane antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prognosis of Goodpasture syndrome has been markedly improved with plasmapheresis, in which the anti-basement membrane antibodies are removed from the plasma, directly addressing the antibody-mediated lung and kidney injury.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibiotics treat infective endocarditis, not the sterile autoimmune injury of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron supplementation does not address the causative autoantibodies even though alveolar hemorrhage occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Allopurinol lowers urate in gout and has no role in Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation targets thrombosis and does not remove the anti-basement membrane antibodies.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has months of fever, fatigue, and weight loss along with chronic sinusitis, bloody nasal discharge, and a saddle-nose deformity. He now has hemoptysis and gross hematuria. Biopsy of a lung nodule shows necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and vessel wall injury. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: The triad of upper airway, lung, and kidney disease with necrotizing granulomas is granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel vasculitis with the classic triad of upper respiratory tract, lung, and kidney disease. Findings include bloody nasal discharge, saddle-nose deformity, lung nodules with hemoptysis, and hematuria, and biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: SLE presents with malar rash, arthritis, and multisystem immune-complex disease rather than necrotizing airway granulomas and saddle-nose deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goodpasture syndrome affects only the lungs and kidneys with linear IgG and lacks sinus disease and granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rheumatoid arthritis is a joint disease and does not cause this upper-airway and renal granulomatous triad.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is a childhood IgA disease with purpura and abdominal pain, not necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy develops palpable purpuric skin lesions over the extensor surfaces of his legs and his buttocks, along with colicky abdominal pain, arthralgias, and microscopic hematuria. Skin biopsy immunofluorescence is most likely to reveal deposition of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgA immune complexes with complement C3

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linear IgG along the basement membrane

explanation.summary: Henoch-Schonlein purpura in a child is caused by deposition of IgA immune complexes with complement C3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Henoch-Schonlein purpura occurs most commonly in children 3-8 years old with purpuric skin lesions on extensor surfaces and buttocks, abdominal pain, arthralgias, and renal abnormalities. Like SLE it results from immune-complex deposition, usually IgA with IgG and complement (C3).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is the immunofluorescence pattern of Goodpasture syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are markers of systemic lupus erythematosus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PR3-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, not HSP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM rheumatoid factor is found in rheumatoid arthritis, not in the purpuric lesions of HSP.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Autoimmune Disease

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl develops fever, swollen and painful knees and ankles, and a new heart murmur approximately 3 weeks after an untreated sore throat. A throat culture obtained at the earlier visit had grown gram-positive cocci arranged in chains. Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis of her current cardiac and joint findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct bacterial seeding of the myocardium and synovium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-reacting with host antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Superantigen-mediated massive cytokine release causing shock

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deposition of preformed bacterial enterotoxin in tissues

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever is an antibody-mediated autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis driven by molecular mimicry.
explanation.whyCorrect: In group A streptococcal infection the M protein is structurally similar to host antigens, so antibodies generated against it cross-react with self-antigens in the heart, joints, skin, and brain. This molecular mimicry produces acute rheumatic fever roughly 2 weeks after the initiating pharyngitis, injuring tissues that were never directly infected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rheumatic fever damages uninfected tissues through the immune response, not by direct bacterial invasion of the heart or joints.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Superantigen-driven cytokine release produces toxic shock, not the delayed autoimmune carditis and arthritis seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enterotoxin-mediated disease (e.g., toxic shock) is a direct toxin effect and does not explain antibody cross-reactivity weeks later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity is not the mechanism of rheumatic fever, which is antibody cross-reaction against self-antigens.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a childhood history of rheumatic fever is found to have a mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex. Echocardiography demonstrates a thickened mitral valve with fused chordae tendineae. Which of the following long-term valvular consequences is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Chronic rheumatic heart disease scars the mitral valve, producing mitral stenosis as an important long-term consequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In rheumatic heart disease the acute endocardial inflammation and vegetations (verrucae) evolve over time into fibrosis, diffuse thickening of the valve leaflets, and fusion of the tendinous cords. This scarring narrows the mitral orifice, and mitral stenosis is described as an important long-term consequence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aortic root dilation is not a described consequence of rheumatic valve scarring, which classically involves the mitral valve.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tricuspid atresia is a congenital malformation, not an acquired consequence of rheumatic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A ventricular septal defect is a congenital septal lesion unrelated to rheumatic valve damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An atrial septal defect is a congenital shunt, not a result of chronic rheumatic leaflet and chordae scarring.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy develops dark, cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and elevated blood pressure 2 weeks after a honey-crusted skin infection. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria, and BUN and serum creatinine are elevated. Electron microscopy of a renal biopsy would most likely reveal which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linear IgG deposition along the basement membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Foot process effacement without immune deposits

choices.label: D
choices.text: Splitting and lamellation of the glomerular basement membrane

explanation.summary: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex disease that produces subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a group A strep infection such as impetigo, scarlet fever, or pharyngitis and results from deposition of immune complexes (streptococcal antigen, antibody, and complement) in the glomeruli. Electron microscopy shows subepithelial 'humps' representing these antigen-antibody complexes, and immunofluorescence highlights granular IgG and C3 deposits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Linear IgG along the basement membrane is characteristic of anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease, not immune-complex PSGN.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foot process effacement without deposits describes minimal change disease, which is not post-infectious.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Basement membrane splitting is seen in hereditary Alport syndrome, not in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nodular Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions are a feature of diabetic nephropathy, unrelated to a preceding streptococcal infection.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy who recently recovered from streptococcal pharyngitis develops involuntary, dance-like movements of the limbs and darting movements of the tongue. Antibodies in this condition are most likely directed against which of the following structures?

explanation.summary: Sydenham chorea results from an autoimmune attack on the basal ganglia after group A streptococcal infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: An autoimmune response against antigens in the basal ganglia produces the subsequent inflammation of Sydenham chorea, classically described as involuntary dance-like movements of the limbs and dart-like movements of the tongue. It is a neurologic consequence of acute rheumatic fever and traditionally resolves over weeks to months.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies against cardiac antigens produce rheumatic carditis, not the movement disorder described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal injury in the post-streptococcal setting is due to immune-complex deposition, not antibodies targeting the movement centers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral nerve myelin is not the described target; chorea reflects central basal ganglia involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, which is unrelated to post-streptococcal chorea.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops conjunctivitis, urethritis, and asymmetric arthritis of the knees several weeks after a diarrheal illness. Arthrocentesis yields sterile synovial fluid, and he is HLA-B27 positive. Which of the following best explains why his arthritis is not expected to respond to antibiotics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The joint inflammation is an immune response to the earlier infection rather than an active joint infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: The causative bacteria are inherently resistant to all antibiotics

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bacteria have formed a protective biofilm within the joint

choices.label: E
choices.text: The arthritis is caused by urate crystal deposition

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis is an immune-mediated, sterile joint inflammation triggered by a prior infection, so antibiotics do not treat the joint disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive arthritis is a classic triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis that follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections. The joint pain is not caused by the infection itself but by an immune response to it, possibly via molecular mimicry, and it is associated with HLA-B27; because the joint is sterile, antibiotics do not resolve the arthritis, which typically resolves within about 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The organisms are not uniquely pan-resistant; the joint simply is not infected, so antibiotics have no target there.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no live biofilm in the joint; the synovial fluid is sterile in reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotic penetration is not the issue because there are no organisms in the joint to eradicate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Crystal deposition causes gout or pseudogout, not the post-infectious triad described here.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with fever and a warm, swollen, painful right knee. Arthrocentesis yields purulent fluid, and Gram stain reveals gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following best characterizes this arthritis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Infectious (septic) arthritis with organisms present in the joint

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reactive arthritis due to molecular mimicry

explanation.summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes an infectious (septic) arthritis in which organisms can be recovered from the joint fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast to Chlamydia, which triggers a reactive arthritis, N. gonorrhoeae causes an infectious (septic) arthritis, and the bacteria can be isolated directly from the synovial fluid. Finding gram-negative diplococci in purulent joint fluid confirms organisms are present within the joint.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reactive arthritis (from Chlamydia or enteric bacteria) produces a sterile joint, whereas here diplococci are seen in the fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A sterile immune-complex arthritis would not show organisms on Gram stain of the synovial fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Crystal-induced arthritis shows crystals, not gram-negative diplococci, in the joint aspirate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulomatous vasculitis is a feature of GPA, not an acute purulent gonococcal joint infection.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: Two gram-negative diplococci are compared. One frequently remains localized to the genital mucosa, whereas the other readily enters the bloodstream from the nasopharynx to cause meningitis and a vasculitic skin rash. Which feature best explains the disseminating organism's ability to evade phagocytosis and spread?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of streptococcal pyogenic exotoxin B

explanation.summary: Neisseria meningitidis has a polysaccharide capsule that helps it escape phagocytosis and disseminate, unlike N. gonorrhoeae.
explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast to N. gonorrhoeae, N. meningitidis possesses a polysaccharide capsule that aids in escaping phagocytosis, so it can more readily enter the bloodstream and spread throughout the body, causing purulent meningitis, vasculitic rash, and pyogenic arthritis. N. gonorrhoeae lacks this capsule and therefore usually remains localized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inability to synthesize ATP describes Chlamydia trachomatis, not the disseminating Neisseria species.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intracytoplasmic inclusions are a feature of Chlamydia trachomatis, not of encapsulated meningococcus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyogenic exotoxin B (SPEB) is a streptococcal antigen involved in PSGN, not a Neisseria virulence factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M protein is a group A streptococcal surface protein, not a feature of Neisseria.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has mucopurulent cervicitis. The causative organism is a gram-negative bacterium that forms intracytoplasmic inclusions and cannot be grown on standard cell-free media. Which of the following best explains why this organism must live inside host cells?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It lacks a cell wall entirely

choices.label: C
choices.text: It requires host antibodies for replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an obligate anaerobe killed by oxygen

choices.label: E
choices.text: It depends on host enzymes to produce its capsule

explanation.summary: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular pathogen because it cannot make its own ATP.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia trachomatis is a gram-negative bacterium that cannot synthesize ATP, an essential energy molecule, so it must live inside cells as an obligate intracellular pathogen. As part of its developmental cycle it forms intracytoplasmic inclusions, and it commonly causes lower genital tract infections such as urethritis and mucopurulent cervicitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chlamydia does have a cell wall; its intracellular dependence stems from its inability to generate ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Host antibodies are part of the immune defense and are not required for chlamydial replication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydia is not described as an obligate anaerobe; its intracellular niche relates to energy dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Its intracellular lifestyle is due to lack of ATP synthesis, not a need for host enzymes to build a capsule.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 32-year-old African-American woman presents with several months of dry cough and dyspnea. Chest imaging shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and biopsy of a lymph node reveals non-necrotizing granulomas with multinucleated giant cells; special stains and cultures for organisms are negative. Which laboratory finding would most support the suspected diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a non-necrotizing granulomatous disease supported by an elevated serum ACE level.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown etiology that classically affects young adults with a higher incidence in women and African-American patients, presenting with cough, dyspnea, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with non-necrotizing granulomas. Because it is a diagnosis of exclusion, an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is a helpful supportive laboratory finding.

whyWrongByChoice.B: PR3-ANCA points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which features necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis, not the sarcoid picture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An elevated anti-streptolysin O titer indicates a preceding streptococcal infection, not sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A positive acid-fast bacilli stain indicates mycobacterial infection and would exclude sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B27 is associated with reactive arthritis and spondyloarthropathies, not with sarcoidosis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A patient with pulmonary granulomas is being evaluated for possible sarcoidosis. Which of the following findings would be INCOMPATIBLE with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis?

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion, so evidence of an infectious cause such as a positive AFB stain is incompatible with it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagnosis of sarcoidosis is one of exclusion, meaning every other possibility for the granulomatous inflammation, especially infectious etiologies, must be excluded. A positive acid-fast bacilli stain indicates mycobacterial infection and would preclude a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Non-necrotizing granulomas are the classic and expected histology of sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are a typical component of sarcoid granulomas and are compatible with the diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythema nodosum is a recognized skin manifestation of sarcoidosis and does not exclude it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An elevated serum ACE level supports, rather than excludes, a diagnosis of sarcoidosis.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with chronic sinusitis and epistaxis, hemoptysis with nodular lung lesions, and a rapidly rising serum creatinine with hematuria. Biopsy shows necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract and small-vessel vasculitis. Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive?

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis mediated by anti-proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA).
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is characterized by the clinical triad of acute necrotizing granulomas of the respiratory tract, granulomatous vasculitis of small-to-medium vessels, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. It is an autoimmune disease mediated by anti-proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA, previously c-ANCA).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-double-stranded DNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, not GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-GBM antibodies cause Goodpasture syndrome, which lacks the necrotizing respiratory granulomas of GPA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-streptolysin O reflects prior streptococcal infection and is unrelated to granulomatous vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with limited scleroderma (CREST), not GPA.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A skin biopsy demonstrates epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding flake-like material that is refractile and appears bright under polarized light. This finding is most consistent with which of the following clinical histories?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Injection of drugs contaminated with talc

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tick bite transmitting a spirochete

explanation.summary: A foreign body granuloma with birefringent flake-like material and giant cells is characteristic of injected talc from IV drug use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foreign body granulomas form around non-digestible material and are identified histologically by histiocytic inflammation with epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells surrounding the material without a T-cell-mediated response. Inhaled or injected drugs such as heroin or cocaine can introduce talc into the tissue, and under polarized light the birefringent talc appears bright, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis leads to immune-mediated sequelae such as rheumatic fever and PSGN, not a birefringent foreign body granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A spirochetal infection can cause a necrotizing infectious granuloma but would not produce birefringent flake-like foreign material.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydia infection is associated with reactive arthritis and cervicitis, not a foreign body granulomatous reaction to injected material.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The described flake-like birefringent material surrounded by giant cells fits injected talc, not the pleural disease produced by asbestos.

questions.topicName: Immune-mediated Damage from Infections and Granulomatous Diseases

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman hospitalized for pneumonia is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. One week later she develops profuse watery diarrhea and crampy abdominal pain. Colonoscopy reveals yellow-white plaques overlying the colonic mucosa. Which of the following best explains why the responsible organism was able to establish this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of the gastric acid barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of the normal gut microbiota by antibiotics

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired mucociliary clearance in the airways

explanation.summary: The normal gut microbiota competes with incoming organisms, and antibiotics disrupt it, permitting Clostridioides difficile overgrowth and pseudomembranous colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The resident gut flora competes with newly arriving organisms for resources and limits colonization. Antibiotics disrupt this microbiota, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and release toxins A and B, which drive cytokine release, neutrophil recruitment, and the pseudomembrane of inflammatory cells and debris.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric acid is a defense against ingested organisms, but the plaques and antibiotic history point to microbiota disruption, not achlorhydria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary clearance is a respiratory tract defense and is unrelated to colonic infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgA deficiency is not the mechanism the brick attributes to antibiotic-associated C. difficile colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urinary obstruction predisposes to urogenital infection, not to pseudomembranous colitis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man develops nausea, crampy abdominal pain, and watery diarrhea two days after a picnic where he ate ham sandwiches and potato salad. Which of the following is the most likely route by which the causative organism entered his body?

explanation.summary: Most gastrointestinal pathogens enter with food or drink contaminated by fecal matter, known as fecal-oral transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most GI pathogens enter with food or drink contaminated by fecal matter (fecal-oral transmission), producing symptoms through toxin production or direct mucosal damage. Foodborne diarrheal illness after a shared meal fits this route.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhalation is the entry route for respiratory pathogens, not for foodborne gastroenteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sexual contact transmits pathogens such as HIV and N. gonorrhoeae, not foodborne diarrheal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percutaneous inoculation involves breaks in the skin, such as bites or needle sticks, not ingestion of food.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retrograde axonal transport moves certain viruses along nerves to the CNS and does not cause food-related diarrhea.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is bitten on the leg by a raccoon while camping. Several weeks later he develops agitation, difficulty swallowing, and a rapidly fatal encephalitis. By which mechanism did the responsible pathogen most likely reach the central nervous system?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct extension across the intact skin

explanation.summary: Some viruses spread along nerves to the CNS by retrograde axonal transport, as seen with rabies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that viruses may spread along nerves to the central nervous system by retrograde axonal transport, listing rabies virus, poliovirus, varicella-zoster virus, and HSV. A fatal encephalitis after an animal bite reflects this neural route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematogenous seeding spreads organisms via blood to sites such as heart valves, not the described neural route to the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphatic spread carries pathogens to lymph nodes before the bloodstream and is not how these neurotropic viruses reach the CNS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pathogen does not extend across intact skin; it enters at the bite wound and travels up nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transplacental transmission passes organisms from mother to fetus and is irrelevant to an animal bite.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who injects heroin presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Blood cultures grow gram-positive cocci, and echocardiography shows a vegetation on the tricuspid valve. Which of the following best describes how the organism reached the heart valve?

explanation.summary: Intravenous drug use can introduce skin bacteria into the bloodstream, which then seed a heart valve, producing endocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that bloodborne dissemination lets pathogens seed distant sites and that endocarditis is a consequence of septicemia. Intravenous drug use with a hypodermic needle introduces bacteria from the skin into the blood, where they lodge on a valve and form a vegetation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retrograde axonal transport carries certain viruses along nerves to the CNS, not bacteria to heart valves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mucociliary mechanisms clear the airways and do not deliver organisms to the endocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fecal-oral ingestion is a route for gastrointestinal pathogens, not for valve seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ascending urethral spread causes urinary tract infection, not endocarditis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and a patent ductus arteriosus. The mother recalls a febrile rash illness during the first trimester. Transmission of the responsible pathogen most likely occurred by which route?

explanation.summary: Placental (transplacental) transmission of TORCH agents such as rubella during pregnancy causes congenital developmental abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes placenta-fetal (vertical) transmission of TORCH infections, which include rubella, and states these cause developmental abnormalities, eye damage, and skin manifestations, often with mild maternal symptoms. First-trimester maternal infection with congenital anomalies fits transplacental spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast milk transmits viruses such as CMV, HIV, and HBV to the newborn but does not explain first-trimester congenital malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Birth canal exposure causes neonatal infections such as gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis, not the congenital triad described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory droplet spread is a person-to-person mode and does not account for prenatal organ malformation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fecal-oral ingestion causes gastrointestinal infection and is unrelated to congenital anomalies.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A tissue biopsy shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages, some fused into multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by a rim of lymphocytes. Which histologic pattern of reaction to injury does this represent?

explanation.summary: Granulomatous inflammation is defined by activated epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells gathered around an insult.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines granulomatous inflammation as a special type of mononuclear inflammation in which activated macrophages gather around an infectious insult, some fusing into multinucleated giant cells; the accumulation is called a granuloma. This matches the described histology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Suppurative inflammation is neutrophil-rich pus, not epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytopathic-cytoproliferative reactions involve single-cell viral changes or cell proliferation, not organized macrophage aggregates.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic scarring is dominated by fibrosis, not by epithelioid macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coagulative infarction reflects ischemic necrosis and is not the granulomatous pattern described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: Autopsy of a patient with pneumonia reveals multiple localized areas of liquefactive necrosis rich in neutrophils, each surrounded by a fibrotic rim. Which type of organism most characteristically produces this pattern of reaction?

explanation.summary: Suppurative inflammation with abscess formation is the hallmark reaction to pyogenic (pus-forming) bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes suppurative (purulent) inflammation as neutrophil-dominated, most commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria, with an abscess defined as localized liquefactive necrosis surrounded by a peripheral fibrotic deposit. This matches the described lung findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Viruses typically produce cytopathic-cytoproliferative or mononuclear reactions, not neutrophilic abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spirochetes such as T. pallidum elicit mononuclear (lymphocytic) inflammation, not suppuration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Helminths characteristically drive mononuclear and eosinophil-rich responses rather than pyogenic abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An autoimmune process would not typically produce this classic pyogenic abscess pattern of infection.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man develops rough, cauliflower-like verrucous growths on his hands. Biopsy shows proliferation of epithelial cells with cytopathic changes. This lesion is an example of which pattern of tissue reaction to infection?

explanation.summary: The cytopathic-cytoproliferative pattern includes viral cell injury and virus-driven cell proliferation, such as HPV warts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the cytopathic-cytoproliferative reaction as involving single cells or small aggregates with cytopathic changes, and notes that some viruses cause cells to proliferate, such as the verrucous warts of human papillomavirus (HPV). The described warty proliferation fits this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Suppurative inflammation is neutrophilic pus formation, not verrucous epithelial proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous inflammation forms epithelioid macrophage aggregates, not virus-induced warts.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caseating necrosis is central cheese-like death seen in tuberculosis granulomas, not proliferative warts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chronic inflammation with scarring produces fibrosis, not the proliferative warty lesion described.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: An unvaccinated child develops a thick gray membrane over the pharynx and, several days later, cardiac arrhythmia. The toxin responsible for this illness damages host cells primarily by which mechanism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acting as a superantigen to trigger cytokine release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Being recognized by macrophages via its Lipid A

explanation.summary: Diphtheria toxin is an A-B toxin whose A subunit inhibits protein synthesis, causing the pharyngeal pseudomembrane and myocarditis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in diphtheria toxin the B component mediates entry by endocytosis and the A component inhibits protein synthesis in the ribosome, leading to cell death; local injury forms the pseudomembrane, and toxin entering the bloodstream can damage myocardial cells to cause acute myocarditis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cleavage of desmoglein-1 is the mechanism of staphylococcal exfoliative toxin, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Superantigen activity is characteristic of staphylococcal enterotoxin and TSST, not diphtheria toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disruption of the enterocyte cytoskeleton describes Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid A recognition describes gram-negative endotoxin, not the A-B diphtheria exotoxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child develops widespread superficial blistering and peeling of the skin following a staphylococcal infection. The toxin responsible for this presentation acts by which mechanism?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forming membrane pores via Lipid A

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein-1, detaching keratinocytes and causing scalded-skin syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that exfoliative A and B toxins produced by S. aureus cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosome protein important for keratinocyte adherence. The resulting detachment compromises the skin barrier, producing staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome with blistering and exfoliation, primarily in pediatric patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Inhibition of protein synthesis is the action of diphtheria toxin, not exfoliative toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipid A pore/immune activation describes gram-negative endotoxin, not the skin-cleaving toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ciliary immobility is associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, not staphylococcal skin disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking neurotransmitter release describes clostridial neurotoxins, not exfoliative toxin.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A young woman develops high fever, hypotension, a diffuse macular rash, and later desquamation of the palms. Cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus from an infected nasal packing. The toxin responsible produces disease by which mechanism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nonspecifically activating many T cells with massive cytokine release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signaling through the Lipid A of lipopolysaccharide

explanation.summary: Superantigen toxins cause toxic shock syndrome by driving nonspecific T-cell activation and a massive cytokine release.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes enterotoxin and TSST as superantigens that stimulate a robust immune response with release of massive amounts of cytokines, and it links toxic shock syndrome to massive cytokine release, including cases from infected nasal packing or postoperative wound materials.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein synthesis inhibition is the diphtheria toxin mechanism, not superantigen action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage of desmosomal proteins describes exfoliative toxin causing scalded-skin syndrome, not TSS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytoskeletal disruption of enterocytes is the mechanism of C. difficile toxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipid A signaling is the mechanism of gram-negative endotoxin, not a staphylococcal superantigen.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A patient with gram-negative bacteremia develops fever and hypotension. The outer membrane component of the bacterium primarily responsible for triggering this systemic response is detected by macrophages through which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Lipid A portion of lipopolysaccharide

explanation.summary: Endotoxin (LPS), particularly its Lipid A portion, is sensed by macrophages and drives fever and cytokine-induced hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also called endotoxin, as an outer membrane component of gram-negative bacteria; its Lipid A portion is detected by immune cells such as macrophages, provoking pro-inflammatory cytokines and complement activation that cause fever and cytokine-induced hypotension.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Peptidoglycan is a cell wall component, but the brick attributes the gram-negative endotoxin response specifically to Lipid A of LPS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Teichoic acid is a gram-positive cell wall component and is not the gram-negative endotoxin described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A-B exotoxins are secreted toxins such as diphtheria toxin, not the outer membrane endotoxin sensed here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Desmoglein-1 is a host desmosomal protein targeted by exfoliative toxin, not a bacterial sensing component.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Infection

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a history of recurrent pneumonia, a liver abscess, and osteomyelitis caused by catalase-positive organisms. Biopsy of an infected lymph node shows granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following best explains this child's recurrent infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defective NADPH oxidase impairing reactive-oxygen-species production

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deficiency of myeloperoxidase in neutrophil granules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation in the LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator gene

explanation.summary: Chronic granulomatous disease results from defective NADPH oxidase, crippling reactive-oxygen-species-dependent intracellular killing.
explanation.whyCorrect: In chronic granulomatous disease, phagocytes cannot generate reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome because NADPH oxidase is defective. Intracellular killing by macrophages and neutrophils fails, so patients suffer recurrent pneumonia, abscesses, lymphadenitis, skin infections, and osteomyelitis, and the defective macrophages accumulate as granulomatous inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Myeloperoxidase deficiency prevents conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid but is usually asymptomatic and does not classically produce granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs integrin-mediated migration and produces infections with absent pus, not reactive-oxygen-species failure with granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Severe congenital neutropenia is defined by too few neutrophils; here the problem is defective killing by phagocytes that are present, as evidenced by granuloma formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A LYST mutation causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which adds partial albinism, neurologic defects, and bleeding rather than isolated granulomatous infection.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child has partial albinism of the skin and hair, recurrent pyogenic infections, easy bruising, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. A peripheral blood smear shows leukocytes containing abnormally large cytoplasmic granules. A defect in which of the following is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lysosomal trafficking regulator protein encoded by the LYST gene

explanation.summary: Chediak-Higashi syndrome arises from a defect in the LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator, producing giant granules that cannot release their contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in the LYST gene encoding a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein. Neutrophils, natural killer cells, and cytotoxic T lymphocytes cannot release toxic granule contents, so patients are vulnerable to infection. Melanosomes cannot release pigment (partial albinism), platelet dense granules cannot be released (bleeding), and lysosomal dysfunction in neurons and glia produces neurologic defects; the giant granules are the diagnostic clue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An NADPH oxidase defect causes chronic granulomatous disease with granulomas, not albinism, giant granules, and bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrin adhesion defects cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency with impaired pus formation, not pigment and platelet-granule abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement deficiency impairs opsonization and lysis but does not cause giant leukocyte granules or albinism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is typically asymptomatic and does not produce albinism, neurologic disease, or giant granules.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with an inherited disorder detected at birth and develops rapidly spreading soft-tissue bacterial infections. Despite severe infection, the involved tissues characteristically show no pus. Which of the following abnormalities best explains these findings?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of oxidative burst within phagolysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability to release cytotoxic granule contents

explanation.summary: Severe congenital neutropenia is defined by a dramatic reduction in neutrophils, so pus is absent even during serious infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe congenital neutropenia is a group of inherited disorders with markedly impaired neutrophil counts, usually diagnosed at birth. Because neutrophils are the key cellular component of a purulent inflammatory response, pus is characteristically absent, and bacteria can spread quickly through soft tissue into the bloodstream.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective oxidative burst describes chronic granulomatous disease; those neutrophils are present and form granulomas rather than being absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inability to release granule contents describes Chediak-Higashi syndrome, which also features albinism and neurologic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deficient hypochlorous acid generation is myeloperoxidase deficiency, which is usually asymptomatic and does not abolish pus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absent membrane attack complex is a complement defect affecting lysis and opsonization, not neutrophil numbers or pus formation.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus develops a severe Candida albicans infection. Laboratory testing reveals an inherited deficiency of a heme-containing enzyme normally present in neutrophil granules; the patient has otherwise been asymptomatic throughout life. Which enzymatic reaction is most likely impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduction of molecular oxygen to superoxide by NADPH oxidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Digestion of bacterial cell walls by lysozyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleavage of complement C3 into C3b

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerization of actin filaments during phagocytosis

explanation.summary: Myeloperoxidase deficiency prevents conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid, usually asymptomatic but linked to Candida infection in diabetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myeloperoxidase is a heme-containing enzyme in neutrophil granules that converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid. Without it, affected cells compensate with other antimicrobial substances, so most patients are asymptomatic; however, severe Candida albicans infections are reported, particularly in the setting of diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired superoxide generation by NADPH oxidase defines chronic granulomatous disease, which is not usually asymptomatic and produces granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme digests bacterial cell walls and is not the heme-containing granule enzyme described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C3 cleavage is a complement function; its deficiency impairs opsonization broadly rather than presenting as isolated Candida infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Actin polymerization supports phagocytic engulfment and is not a heme-dependent oxidative killing step.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A virus infecting a host epithelial cell downregulates expression of MHC class I molecules to avoid recognition by cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Despite this, the infected cell is still killed. Which of the following cells is most likely responsible, and by what mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Natural killer cells detecting absent MHC class I and releasing perforin and granzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutrophils generating hypochlorous acid within phagolysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plasma cells secreting neutralizing antibodies against the viral capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD4-positive helper T cells directly lysing the infected cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Eosinophils releasing major basic protein onto the cell surface

explanation.summary: Natural killer cells sense loss of MHC class I and kill virus-infected cells non-specifically via perforin and granzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: A common viral evasion strategy is downregulation of class I MHC to escape cytotoxic T cells. Natural killer cells sense the lack of class I MHC and kill the virus-infected cell non-specifically by secreting perforins and proteolytic granzymes, driving the cell into apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophil oxidative killing targets phagocytosed microbes, not host cells that have lost surface MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies neutralize extracellular virus and opsonize, but they do not exploit the absence of MHC class I to kill an infected cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4-positive helper T cells coordinate responses through cytokines; they are not the direct cytolytic effectors that respond to missing MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eosinophils act mainly against helminths and are not the effectors that kill MHC-class-I-negative virus-infected cells.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: During replication, a virus generates double-stranded RNA within an infected cell. In response, the cell produces and releases interferons that act on neighboring cells to establish an antiviral state. Which of the following best describes how these interferons block viral protein synthesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate enzymes that degrade mRNA and inhibit eIF-2 in the presence of double-stranded RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind viral gp120 and prevent attachment to CD4 receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: They insert a membrane attack complex into the viral envelope

choices.label: D
choices.text: They opsonize virions to enhance phagocytosis by macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: They cross-link viral capsid proteins to prevent uncoating

explanation.summary: Interferons induce enzymes that, in the presence of double-stranded RNA, halt protein synthesis and thereby block viral replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Interferons are released from infected cells in response to double-stranded RNA present during viral replication. They activate 2'-5' oligoadenylate synthetase, which induces a ribonuclease that degrades mRNA, and they activate protein kinase R, which inhibits the initiation factor eIF-2. Both actions stop protein synthesis and prevent production of new virus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gp120-CD4 binding is a mechanism relevant to HIV entry, not the antiviral action of interferons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The membrane attack complex is a complement structure that lyses cells and microbes; it is not how interferons work.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is a complement- and antibody-mediated process, not an interferon-induced block of protein synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Interferons do not cross-link capsid proteins; they act intracellularly to shut down translation.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops a febrile illness after eating unpasteurized dairy products, and her neonate is subsequently born with disseminated infection and meningitis. The responsible gram-positive bacillus survives inside host cells and spreads directly from one cell to the next without re-entering the extracellular space. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this intracellular survival and spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Listeriolysin O ruptures the phagosome and actin polymerization propels the organism between cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polysaccharide capsule blocks complement deposition on the bacterial surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG to prevent opsonization

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigenic variation of surface pili avoids antibody recognition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Downregulation of MHC class I prevents cytotoxic T-cell killing

explanation.summary: Listeria monocytogenes escapes the phagosome via listeriolysin O and uses actin-based motility to spread cell-to-cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listeria monocytogenes is a gram-positive bacillus acquired from dairy and milk products that can cross the placenta and cause disseminated neonatal infection and meningitis. After being taken up, it escapes the phagosome using listeriolysin O, a pore-forming toxin, before phagolysosomal killing occurs. It then propels itself through the cell by polymerizing actin filaments (ActA), protruding into and entering the next cell, so it spreads without re-entering the extracellular space.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis extracellularly and does not explain cytoplasmic escape and actin-based spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus mechanism that blocks opsonization, not intracellular motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antigenic variation of pili is a Neisseria strategy against antibodies, unrelated to phagosomal escape.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a viral evasion tactic, not the mechanism used by this intracellular bacterium.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense
