questions.stem: A strain of Staphylococcus aureus expresses a surface protein that binds the Fc portion of IgG antibodies. As a result, IgG bound to the bacterium can no longer engage Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages. Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired antibody-mediated phagocytosis of the bacterium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of natural killer cell recognition of infected host cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of interferon-induced antiviral protein synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of phagolysosome formation within macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antigenic variation of the bacterial surface proteins

explanation.summary: Staphylococcal Protein A binds IgG by its Fc region, preventing the antibody from directing phagocytes to the bacterium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Staphylococcus aureus expresses Protein A, which binds the Fc portion of IgG. Because the Fc region is what normally engages Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, this binding prevents the bound IgG from triggering phagocytosis, so antibody-mediated (opsonic) clearance of the bacterium is impaired.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural killer cell recognition depends on MHC class I status of host cells, not on IgG binding to a bacterial surface protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interferon-induced antiviral responses are unrelated to this antibody-blocking mechanism used against a bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting phagolysosome formation is a strategy of intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria, not the effect of Protein A.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antigenic variation involves changing surface antigens; Protein A instead blocks the antibody's effector function directly.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A patient develops repeated infections with Neisseria despite generating antibodies against the organism during each episode. Analysis shows that the bacterium expresses new pilin surface proteins over time by placing different pilin coding sequences next to a single promoter. Which of the following best describes the mechanism responsible for this immune evasion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigenic variation through homologous recombination of pilin genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secretion of a polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binding of the Fc portion of IgG by a surface protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Escape from the phagosome using a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Downregulation of host MHC class I molecules

explanation.summary: Neisseria evades adaptive immunity by antigenic variation, using homologous recombination to swap pilin variants next to its promoter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neisseria carries 10-15 silent pilin protein variants and expresses only the one situated next to the promoter. Through homologous recombination, a new pilin coding sequence is placed next to the promoter, so a new pilin protein is expressed that antibodies raised against the previous variant no longer recognize. This antigenic variation allows the organism to escape the antibody response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule resists phagocytosis but does not explain the sequential change in pilin antigens described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the Protein A mechanism of Staphylococcus aureus, not pilin antigenic variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pore-forming phagosomal escape is used by Listeria; it does not change surface antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a viral strategy against T cells, not a bacterial antibody-evasion mechanism.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A virus uses its surface glycoprotein gp120, together with the chemokine co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4, to bind and enter a specific population of host cells. Over time, destruction of these cells leaves the patient in an immunosuppressed state and vulnerable to opportunistic infections. Which host cells does this virus preferentially infect?

explanation.summary: HIV shows tropism for CD4-positive helper T cells because gp120 binds CD4 with the co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human immunodeficiency virus utilizes gp120 to bind CD4 and the chemokine co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4 to enter and infect the cell. This gives the virus tropism for CD4-positive cells, known as helper T cells. Their infection and destruction leaves the patient immunosuppressed and vulnerable to other infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Natural killer cells lack the CD4-based entry receptor and are not the target population defined by gp120 tropism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are not CD4-positive helper T cells and are not preferentially infected via gp120-CD4 binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mature B lymphocytes are not the CD4-positive helper T cells targeted by gp120 and its co-receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although macrophages can be infected, the specific tropism described by gp120 binding to CD4 with CCR5/CXCR4 defines helper T cells, not macrophages exclusively.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A pathogenic fungus proliferating in a patient's tissues secretes abundant capsular material, and a co-infecting bacterium is likewise surrounded by a thick polysaccharide coat. Neither organism is efficiently cleared by neutrophils or macrophages. Which of the following best explains how the capsule promotes immune evasion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It interferes with complement deposition and phagocytosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It degrades host mRNA to block protein synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It binds the Fc portion of IgG to block Fc receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits interferon release from infected cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It downregulates MHC class I on host cells

explanation.summary: Polysaccharide capsules interfere with complement deposition and phagocytosis, letting encapsulated microbes evade professional phagocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Polysaccharide capsules interfere with complement deposition and phagocytosis. Encapsulated bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae and certain fungi like Cryptococcus neoformans exploit this; Cryptococcus even secretes capsule material to inhibit immune attack, allowing the organisms to resist engulfment by neutrophils and macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Degrading host mRNA describes an interferon-induced antiviral action, not the function of a microbial capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding the Fc portion of IgG is the staphylococcal Protein A mechanism, not a property of the polysaccharide capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting interferon release is a viral tactic and does not explain capsule-mediated resistance to phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MHC class I downregulation is a strategy of viruses, not of encapsulated bacteria and fungi.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A child has recurrent bacterial infections in which the affected sites conspicuously fail to form pus, and neutrophils are found to remain within the bloodstream rather than migrating into infected tissues. Which of the following defects best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Impaired integrin-mediated adhesion of leukocytes to endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective NADPH oxidase in the phagolysosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inability to release cytotoxic granules due to a LYST mutation

explanation.summary: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs integrin-mediated adhesion, so leukocytes cannot migrate into tissue and pus fails to form.
explanation.whyCorrect: For leukocytes to leave the bloodstream and migrate into tissues, integrins are needed for adhesion to endothelial cells. In leukocyte adhesion deficiency, impaired integrin function prevents this adhesion and migration, so infections recur and the affected sites fail to form pus despite serious infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A defective oxidative burst causes chronic granulomatous disease; those neutrophils reach tissue and form granulomas rather than failing to migrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase deficiency impairs hypochlorous acid generation and is usually asymptomatic, not a defect of leukocyte migration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A LYST mutation causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome with giant granules, albinism, and bleeding, not an isolated adhesion/migration defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absent complement opsonization reduces microbial coating and lysis but does not trap neutrophils in the bloodstream.

questions.topicName: Infections, Immunity, and Evading Host Defense

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with several months of cough and weight loss undergoes lung biopsy. When the tissue is stained and then treated with acid-alcohol, slender rod-shaped organisms retain the stain and appear pink. Which structural feature is most responsible for this staining property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A waxy cell wall containing mycolic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ability to form dormant endospores

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis is acid-fast because of mycolic acid in its cell wall.
explanation.whyCorrect: M. tuberculosis is an aerobic rod with a waxy cell wall that includes mycolic acid. This feature causes the organism to retain stain after treatment with acid-alcohol, which is why it is called acid-fast and is highlighted by the acid-fast bacilli (AFB) special stain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule is a virulence feature of other bacteria and does not account for acid-fastness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lipopolysaccharide outer membrane characterizes gram-negative bacteria, not the acid-fast mycobacterial wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corkscrew morphology describes the spirochete Treponema pallidum, not M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M. tuberculosis does not form endospores; its stain retention is due to mycolic acid.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: M. tuberculosis is phagocytosed by a nonactivated alveolar macrophage but is not destroyed and instead replicates inside the cell. Which mechanism best explains how the organism avoids intracytoplasmic killing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It prevents phagolysosome formation and halts acidification and reactive oxygen species production

choices.label: B
choices.text: It secretes an IgA protease that cleaves mucosal antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: It integrates its genome into the host cell DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: It forms spores that resist lysosomal enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses corkscrew motility to escape into the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: M. tuberculosis survives in macrophages by blocking phagolysosome maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: After entering nonactivated macrophages via mannose-binding lectin and CR3, M. tuberculosis avoids intracytoplasmic killing by preventing phagolysosomal formation and by halting acidification and reactive oxygen species production. It is then left to replicate within the protection of the intracellular vesicle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA protease is a mucosal evasion strategy of other pathogens and is not the mechanism described here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genome integration is characteristic of certain viruses, not of M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. tuberculosis does not form spores; it blocks phagolysosome function instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corkscrew motility describes Treponema pallidum, not intracellular mycobacterial survival.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with active pulmonary tuberculosis has a lung lesion resected. On gross examination the lesion is friable, cheesy, and white; microscopically there is central necrosis surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells. Which term best describes this classic histologic feature of active tuberculosis?

explanation.summary: Caseating granulomas are the classic histologic finding of active tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ongoing immune attack against M. tuberculosis within granulomas produces necrosis, manifesting as caseating granulomas. These are friable, cheesy, and white grossly, and show central necrosis with epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells microscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythema nodosum refers to painful red nodules of the lower extremities that may rarely accompany primary tuberculosis, not the granuloma itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis is a nonspecific reparative change seen in many processes, including healing mycobacterial disease, but it is not the classic active lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gummas are granulomatous nodules of tertiary syphilis, not tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Condylomata lata are elevated plaques of secondary syphilis, unrelated to tuberculosis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A healthcare worker receives an intradermal injection of tuberculin. Because she was exposed to tuberculosis in the past, an erythematous, indurated reaction develops at the injection site 48 to 72 hours later. This reaction is mediated by which type of hypersensitivity?

explanation.summary: The tuberculin (PPD) skin test reflects a Type IV, Th1 cell-mediated response.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a person has been exposed to tuberculosis, injecting tuberculin triggers a cell-mediated Th1-cell response, a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction, producing an erythematous reaction at the injection site within 48 to 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I reactions are immediate and IgE-mediated, occurring within minutes, not over 48 to 72 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type II involves antibody directed against cell-surface antigens, which is not the basis of the delayed skin test.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type III involves immune complex deposition and does not explain the delayed T-cell reaction to tuberculin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reaction is an adaptive T-cell response, not a purely innate complement-mediated one.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: After tuberculosis antigens drain into lymph nodes, a pro-inflammatory cytokine stimulates naive T-cells to differentiate into T helper type 1 (Th1) cells, which then coordinate the antimycobacterial response. Which cytokine drives this Th1 differentiation?

explanation.summary: IL-12 promotes differentiation of naive T-cells into Th1 cells in tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tuberculosis antigens draining into lymph nodes trigger production of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-12, which stimulates naive T-cells to differentiate into Th1 cells. Th1 cells then produce IFN-gamma to activate macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation, which is not the protective response emphasized against M. tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-5 supports eosinophil responses, not Th1 differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is generally immunosuppressive and dampens, rather than drives, the Th1 response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta has regulatory and fibrotic roles and does not promote Th1 differentiation here.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV develops fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis years after a resolved primary tuberculosis infection. Chest imaging shows cavitary disease. In this reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis, the lesions most characteristically involve which location?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The upper apices of the lungs

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right hilar lymph nodes only

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pleural space without lung involvement

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lung bases with a peripheral wedge shape

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vertebral bodies of the spine

explanation.summary: Secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis characteristically involves the upper lung apices.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary pulmonary tuberculosis tends to manifest in the upper apices of the lungs. Because the immune system is already primed, it prompts a robust response with erosion and cavitation of lung parenchyma and fibrosis, and symptoms include night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Right hilar lymphadenopathy is a feature of primary tuberculosis, not the apical cavitary lesions of reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pleural effusions can occur, but secondary disease characteristically involves the upper lung apices, not isolated pleura.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A basilar wedge-shaped lesion is not the classic pattern of secondary tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebral involvement describes Pott disease, an extrapulmonary form, not the typical apical reactivation site.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 60-year-old immunocompromised man dies of an overwhelming infection. At autopsy the spleen, liver, and bone marrow are studded with numerous small tan-white tubercles resembling scattered millet seeds. Which process best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Widespread millet-seed-like tubercles across multiple organs indicate miliary tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term miliary refers to the resemblance to millet seeds and describes unchecked tuberculosis that accesses the lymphatic and venous blood supplies, seeding organs such as the lung, liver, bone marrow, spleen, adrenal glands, or kidneys. Progressive dissemination throughout the bloodstream to multiple organs is termed systemic miliary tuberculosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Latent tuberculosis is asymptomatic and contained, without widespread organ seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary tuberculosis is the first, often unrecognized infection and does not usually produce disseminated millet-seed nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pott disease is isolated vertebral tuberculosis, not multiorgan seeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythema nodosum refers to tender skin nodules, not disseminated organ tubercles.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with a single genital lesion that appeared about three weeks after unprotected intercourse. The lesion is solitary, painless, erythematous, and has a sharp border with an ulcerative base. Which finding is most suggestive of primary syphilis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A maculopapular rash of the palms and soles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raised, moist tan-white plaques of intertriginous areas

explanation.summary: The chancre, a solitary painless ulcer, is the key finding of primary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The chancre is the key clinical finding in primary syphilis. It is usually solitary, occurs at the site of the original infection (often the genitals), and is painless and erythematous, typically with a sharp border and an ulcerative base, appearing about three weeks after infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A maculopapular rash of the palms and soles is characteristic of secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple painful vesicles suggest herpes simplex virus infection, not the painless syphilitic chancre.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Annular plaques of the face are described in secondary syphilis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Raised moist plaques of intertriginous areas are condylomata lata, a feature of secondary syphilis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops a symmetric maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, along with moist elevated plaques in the anogenital region and mild fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. Her genital ulcer resolved several weeks earlier. Which stage of syphilis does this presentation represent?

explanation.summary: A palm-and-sole rash with condylomata lata and constitutional symptoms marks secondary syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary syphilis manifests 2 to 8 weeks after the chancre and is characterized by multiple lesions, including maculopapular rashes often of the palms and soles, and condylomata lata (elevated plaques of intertriginous areas). Constitutional signs include sore throat, lymphadenopathy, mild fever, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary syphilis is defined by a single painless chancre, which had already resolved in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Latent syphilis is continued infection in the absence of clinical symptoms, not an active rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tertiary syphilis appears years later with gummas, cardiovascular, or neurologic disease, not an acute rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital syphilis results from vertical transmission to a fetus, not this adult presentation.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a remote history of untreated syphilis is found to have a new diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation and imaging showing dilation of the aortic root and an ascending aortic aneurysm. Which process best accounts for these cardiovascular findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aortitis causing dilation of the aortic root and arch

explanation.summary: Cardiovascular tertiary syphilis causes aortitis with root dilation, regurgitation, and aneurysm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiovascular syphilis accounts for most cases of tertiary syphilis. Inflammation of the aorta leads to dilation of the aortic root and arch, resulting in valvular insufficiency and aortic regurgitation, and aneurysms can form in the aorta, predisposing to dissection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral stenosis from rheumatic disease is a distinct valvular process not caused by syphilitic aortitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although coronary ostial stenosis can occur in syphilis, atherosclerotic plaque rupture is a separate mechanism and does not explain the aortic root dilation and regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension does not produce aortic root dilation or aortic regurgitation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral pericarditis causes an effusion, not aortic root dilation, aneurysm, and regurgitation.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is brought in for progressive memory and judgment decline. On exam his pupils are small and, although they constrict when he focuses on a finger held near his nose, they do not react to light. He also has red-purple facial nodules containing friable tan-yellow material. Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: Argyll Robertson pupils, dementia, and facial gummas point to tertiary neurosyphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Argyll Robertson pupil accommodates to near objects but does not react to light and is a classic sign of advanced (tertiary) syphilis. Paretic neurosyphilis follows T. pallidum invasion of the brain with progressive cognitive decline, and the friable facial nodules are gummas of tertiary syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary syphilis presents with a painless chancre, not dementia and pupillary abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secondary syphilis features rashes and constitutional symptoms, not Argyll Robertson pupils and gummas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent syphilis is asymptomatic by definition, so it cannot explain these active neurologic findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculous meningitis does not produce Argyll Robertson pupils or cutaneous gummas.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child born to a mother with untreated syphilis has notched, peg-shaped teeth, clouding of the cornea from interstitial keratitis, and progressive hearing loss. Which finding is characteristic of congenital syphilis rather than acquired adult syphilis?

explanation.summary: Hutchinson (notched) teeth are a late finding specific to congenital syphilis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Late congenital syphilis may manifest as interstitial keratitis, eighth cranial nerve deafness, and bone or teeth abnormalities. Notched or peg-shaped teeth, called Hutchinson teeth, are characteristic of congenital syphilis and are not a feature of acquired adult syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Condylomata lata may be seen in secondary syphilis or congenital syphilis, so they are not specific to congenital disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A painless chancre is the hallmark of acquired primary syphilis in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gummas occur in tertiary (adult) syphilis and can also occur congenitally, so they are not specific to the congenital form.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A maculopapular rash occurs in both secondary and congenital syphilis and is therefore not distinguishing.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (1 of 2): Tuberculosis and Syphilis

questions.stem: A 24-year-old hiker in Connecticut develops a single, slowly expanding annular red skin lesion with central clearing on the thigh about one week after a tick bite. The lesion resembles a bullseye. Which of the following is the most likely dermatologic finding?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans is the classic skin finding of early localized Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Borrelia burgdorferi, transmitted by the Ixodes deer tick, produces an annular erythematous rash with a pale center that resembles a bullseye, known as erythema migrans. It appears in the early localized stage and usually resolves within 4-12 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythema marginatum is the serpiginous rash of acute rheumatic fever following Group A streptococcal infection, not Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythema nodosum is nonspecific tender red nodules on the lower extremities seen in conditions such as tuberculosis and sarcoidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythema multiforme presents with targetoid lesions typically triggered by infections such as HSV or by drugs, not by B. burgdorferi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrolytic migratory erythema is associated with glucagonoma, an unrelated endocrine tumor.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: Despite the generation of specific antibodies over several weeks, Borrelia burgdorferi persists in an infected host. The organism shuttles different sequences of an outer surface lipoprotein (VlsE) next to a single gene promoter for expression. This strategy best illustrates which of the following mechanisms of immune evasion?

explanation.summary: B. burgdorferi escapes antibody-mediated attack by antigenic variation of its VlsE lipoprotein.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that B. burgdorferi possesses multiple alternate sequences of the surface lipoprotein VlsE next to a single promoter. Only the sequence adjacent to the promoter is expressed, so different variants can be shuttled in to express alternate VlsE proteins and escape immune recognition. This is antigenic variance (variation).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The described mechanism involves changing a surface protein while extracellular, not hiding inside host cells as a latent form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Molecular mimicry means resembling host antigens; here the organism actively changes its own antigen rather than imitating the host.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Superantigens nonspecifically activate large numbers of T cells and are not the mechanism of VlsE switching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA and is a feature of certain respiratory pathogens, not the VlsE variation described.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man reports several weeks of migratory joint pain, palpitations, and a stiff neck. He recalls a bullseye rash that faded a few weeks earlier. Physical exam reveals lymphadenopathy and an irregular heart rhythm. These findings are most consistent with which stage of Lyme disease?

explanation.summary: Cardiac arrhythmias, lymphocytic meningitis, and multisystem signs days to weeks after erythema migrans define early disseminated Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early disseminated disease follows hematogenous spread of B. burgdorferi days to weeks after erythema migrans. The brick lists constitutional symptoms, multiple erythema migrans, lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, migratory joint/muscle pain, cardiac arrhythmias, and nervous system involvement such as lymphocytic meningitis and nerve dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early localized disease is characterized by a solitary erythema migrans lesion without dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Late disseminated disease occurs months later and is dominated by large-joint arthritis, not this acute multisystem picture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late localized disease is not a recognized stage of Lyme disease and serves as a distractor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital Lyme disease is not the entity described; this is an adult with recent tick exposure and dissemination.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who never received treatment for a tick-borne illness months earlier now presents with swelling and pain of both knees. Arthrocentesis shows inflammatory fluid, and there is ongoing synovial inflammation. Which stage of Lyme disease does this presentation most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Large-joint arthritis from synovial inflammation months after untreated infection marks late disseminated Lyme disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that months after infection, untreated patients may progress to late disseminated (persistent) disease, which is usually dominated by large-joint arthritis due to ongoing synovial inflammation and damage. Chronic neurologic changes may rarely occur.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early localized disease features a solitary erythema migrans lesion days after the bite, not chronic arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Early disseminated disease occurs days to weeks after erythema migrans and features migratory pains, carditis, and meningitis rather than persistent large-joint arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute retroviral syndrome is an HIV entity, not a Lyme stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary infection with viremia describes HIV dissemination, unrelated to Borrelia joint disease.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A researcher studies the virus responsible for AIDS and notes that its genome consists of two RNA molecules and that it synthesizes DNA from viral RNA within the cells it infects. This enzymatic activity is the reason the virus is classified in which of the following groups?

explanation.summary: HIV is a retrovirus because it uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA from its RNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes HIV as a virus with a genome of two (diploid) RNA molecules, a capsid, and an envelope. It is referred to as a retrovirus because it uses reverse transcriptase to synthesize DNA from viral RNA within the infected cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV is an RNA virus; it only produces DNA secondarily through reverse transcription and is not itself a double-stranded DNA virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prions are misfolded proteins with no nucleic acid genome, unlike HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is enveloped, not a non-enveloped virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacteriophages infect bacteria, whereas HIV infects human CD4+ T cells.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with known HIV infection is being staged. His most recent CD4+ T-cell count is 150 cells/microL. Which of the following best explains why he now meets criteria for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4+ T-cell count less than 200 cells/microL

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4+ T-cell count of 500 cells/microL or greater

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detectable HIV-1 RNA in the blood

explanation.summary: For adults, AIDS is defined as a CD4+ T-cell count below 200 cells/microL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that AIDS is defined as a CD4+ T-cell count of less than 200/microL and corresponds to HIV Stage 3. This profound immunosuppression leaves the patient vulnerable to opportunistic infections, secondary neoplasms, and neurologic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A count of 200-499 cells/microL corresponds to HIV Stage 2, which does not meet AIDS criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A count of 500 or more cells/microL corresponds to HIV Stage 1, the earliest stage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Detectable HIV-1 RNA marks active viral replication and is useful for monitoring but does not by itself define AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-HIV antibodies indicate infection but do not define the AIDS stage; the CD4 count does.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man develops sore throat, myalgia, fever, and fatigue about 3 weeks after a high-risk sexual exposure. Symptoms resolve spontaneously over the next few weeks. Around this time, virus-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells appear and detectable viral titers fall. This clinical picture is most consistent with which phase of HIV infection?

explanation.summary: A self-limited mononucleosis-like illness weeks after exposure, coinciding with rising CD8+ CTLs, is the acute retroviral syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that virus-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells appear within 3-7 weeks of exposure, corresponding to a drop in viral titers (the first equilibrium point). Acute retroviral syndrome is the initial, usually nonspecific presentation with sore throat, myalgia, fever, weight loss, and fatigue that resolves in 2-4 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The chronic phase is clinically latent and largely asymptomatic, following the acute syndrome rather than presenting as an acute febrile illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clinical AIDS reflects profound immunosuppression with opportunistic infections and neoplasms, not a transient early illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Late disseminated disease is a stage of Lyme disease, not HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is a late neurologic complication of advanced AIDS, not the acute seroconversion illness.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a CD4+ T-cell count of 90 cells/microL presents with progressive dyspnea and a nonproductive cough. CT of the chest shows diffuse ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage is performed, and a Gomori methenamine silver stain highlights cyst walls as dark gray organisms. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?

explanation.summary: Ground-glass opacities plus GMS-positive cysts on BAL in an AIDS patient indicate Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes Pneumocystis jirovecii as a ubiquitous fungus that is asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts but causes pneumonia in AIDS, with dyspnea and nonproductive cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray, and diffuse ground-glass opacities on CT. Bronchoalveolar lavage with GMS staining highlights the cyst walls, confirming the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in AIDS classically causes retinitis, colitis, and meningoencephalitis rather than GMS-positive cystic organisms on lavage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tuberculosis is a bacterial opportunistic infection and would not show silver-staining cyst walls on BAL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasma gondii causes ring-enhancing brain lesions, not this pulmonary cyst picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV in AIDS typically produces mucocutaneous or perirectal ulceration, not diffuse ground-glass pneumonia with cysts.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with untreated AIDS develops progressive vision loss in one eye. Ophthalmoscopic examination reveals retinal hemorrhage and inflammation. Which of the following opportunistic pathogens is the most likely cause of her blindness?

explanation.summary: CMV retinitis is an important cause of blindness in AIDS, with retinal hemorrhage and inflammation on fundoscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that CMV reactivation in immunosuppressed patients can cause severe infections including CMV colitis, meningoencephalitis, and retinitis, the last being an important cause of blindness with inflammation and hemorrhage seen on ophthalmoscopic examination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia, not retinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Human herpesvirus-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not retinal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a white matter disease, not retinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Candida albicans typically causes oral or vaginal candidiasis in this setting rather than hemorrhagic retinitis.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with AIDS presents with headache and focal neurologic deficits. MRI of the brain shows multiple enhancing, ring-like lesions. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for these findings?

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS classically indicate toxoplasmic encephalitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that although primary Toxoplasma gondii infection is usually asymptomatic in immunocompetent hosts, in AIDS patients it can cause toxoplasmic encephalitis with multiple enhancing, ring-like lesions on MRI. These correspond to multiple abscesses and necrotic foci on neuropathologic examination.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in AIDS causes retinitis, colitis, and meningoencephalitis rather than the classic multiple ring-enhancing lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia, not focal brain lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with B-cell lymphomas, which would appear as mass lesions but are not the classic toxoplasmosis ring-enhancing picture described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, not ring-enhancing brain abscesses in AIDS.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with advanced HIV infection develops multiple violaceous patches and plaques on the chest and oral mucosa. Biopsy shows a proliferation of bland, ovoid-to-spindled endothelial cells. This vascular neoplasm is most strongly associated with which of the following viruses?

explanation.summary: Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular endothelial tumor, is associated with human herpesvirus-8 (HHV8).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that HHV8 infection is associated with Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular neoplasm that manifests as multiple cutaneous, mucosal, or visceral lesions and is composed of proliferating endothelial cells (bland, ovoid-to-spindled cells on microscopy).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Epstein-Barr virus is associated with B-cell lymphomas such as a subset of diffuse large B-cell and Hodgkin lymphoma, not the vascular endothelial tumor described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytomegalovirus causes retinitis, colitis, and encephalitis, not Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV-1 causes mucocutaneous ulcerations, not an endothelial neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, not a vascular tumor.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS develops progressive weakness and cognitive decline. MRI shows white matter lesions, and brain tissue demonstrates demyelination with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei in infected glial cells. The responsible virus preferentially infects which cell type to produce this demyelinating disease?

explanation.summary: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy results from JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes, causing demyelination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes JC virus-induced progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy as an AIDS-associated demyelinating disease. The JC virus infects oligodendrocytes, which are responsible for the production and maintenance of myelin, so their infection leads to loss of myelin (white matter lesions) with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV itself infects CD4+ T lymphocytes, but the demyelinating JC virus targets oligodendrocytes, not T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endothelial cells are the target in Kaposi sarcoma, not in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retinal photoreceptors are affected in CMV retinitis, not in JC virus disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type II pneumocytes are lung cells and are not the target of the JC virus.

questions.topicName: Chronic Infections (2 of 2): Lyme Disease and HIV/AIDS

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with end-stage renal disease receives a kidney donated by his identical twin brother. Which of the following terms best describes this type of graft?

explanation.summary: An isograft is tissue transferred between genetically identical individuals of the same species, such as identical twins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an isograft as tissue transferred between individuals of the same species who are genetically identical. Because identical twins share the same genome, a transplant between them is an isograft, which minimizes the risk of immune rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An allograft is between genetically different individuals of the same species, not identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An autograft transfers tissue from one body site to another on the same individual, not between two people.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is between different species, such as animal tissue placed into a human.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homograft is not one of the four graft types defined in this brick (autograft, isograft, allograft, xenograft).

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhosis receives a liver from a deceased, genetically unrelated human donor. Which of the following terms best describes this type of graft, which represents the most common transplant performed in medicine?

explanation.summary: An allograft is tissue transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species and is the most common transplant type.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that an allograft is tissue transferred between genetically different individuals of the same species. Because most donors and recipients are non-identical humans, allografting is the most common transplant performed in medicine.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An autograft moves tissue from one part of a patient's body to another on the same person.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An isograft is between genetically identical individuals such as identical twins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A xenograft is between different species, not two humans.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intergraft is a horticultural term for grafting plants, not a category of human transplantation.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant team struggles to find a compatible donor for a patient because of the extremely high genetic variability (polymorphism) of a particular gene family. Which of the following genes is most responsible for making the donor-recipient matching process so difficult?

explanation.summary: HLA genes are highly polymorphic, which makes finding a compatible donor difficult.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes that HLA genes have high genetic variability (polymorphism), which often makes it difficult to find compatible donors. HLA genes encode MHC molecules used to distinguish self from non-self, and mismatches drive rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABO genes are important in matching but are not highly polymorphic like HLA genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-1 is a circulating cytokine of inflammation; its gene is not involved in transplant compatibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgE is an antibody notable in type 1 hypersensitivity, not transplant matching.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antinuclear antibodies are seen in autoimmune disease such as lupus and are not involved in transplant compatibility.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: The HLA gene complex is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 and is organized into three classes. Which of the following correctly pairs an HLA class with the genes it contains?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Class I contains HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class I contains HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Class II contains HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Class II encodes cytokines rather than MHC molecules

explanation.summary: Class I HLA genes are HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C; class II genes are HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the brick, there are three class I HLA genes (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) and three class II HLA genes (HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, HLA-DR). Both class I and class II genes encode MHC molecules and are critical to transplant matching.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR are class II genes, not class I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C are class I genes, not class II.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Class III genes encode other molecules such as cytokines and do not contain HLA-DR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class II genes encode MHC molecules; it is the class III genes that encode cytokines.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: An organ procurement organization notes that a deceased donor's blood type lacks A and B antigens, allowing donation to recipients of any ABO type. Which of the following blood types did this donor most likely have?

explanation.summary: Type O individuals lack A and B antigens, making them universal donors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that people with type O blood do not have A or B antigens on their red blood cells. Because recipient anti-AB antibodies will not react against O-type cells, type O donors are considered 'universal' transplant donors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type A blood carries the A antigen, which would react with anti-A antibodies in some recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type B blood carries the B antigen, which would react with anti-B antibodies in some recipients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type AB carries both A and B antigens and is the least universal donor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rh status refers to a separate antigen system and does not define the universal donor concept described here for ABO.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 40-year-old kidney transplant recipient is started on an immunosuppressive medication that prevents rejection specifically by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation. Which of the following drugs is most consistent with this mechanism of action?

explanation.summary: Mycophenolate mofetil is an immunosuppressant that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifically states that mycophenolate mofetil inhibits lymphocyte proliferation, whereas tacrolimus inhibits T-cell responses. Blocking lymphocyte proliferation dampens the recipient immune response against the graft.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tacrolimus inhibits T-cell responses rather than acting primarily by blocking lymphocyte proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Steroids such as prednisone are broad anti-inflammatory immunosuppressants and are not described as inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation specifically.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IVIG is used to treat rejection, not as a maintenance drug that inhibits lymphocyte proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasmapheresis removes offending antibodies from the circulation and is a treatment for rejection, not a lymphocyte-proliferation inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis is being ranked for a liver transplant. Her physician calculates a numeric score from her bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and INR to determine medical urgency. Which of the following scores is being used?

explanation.summary: The MELD score ranks liver transplant urgency in patients age 12 or older using bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and INR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score as a numeric score used in patients age 12 or older that includes bilirubin, sodium, albumin, creatinine, and prothrombin time expressed as INR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The PELD score is used in patients younger than 12 and includes height and weight, which are not listed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Status 1 is a categorical highest-priority designation for fulminant failure, not a numeric score calculated from these labs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphocyte cross-matching detects recipient antibodies against donor lymphocytes; it is not a liver urgency score.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extended criteria donor refers to risk features of a deceased donor, not a recipient urgency score.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops fulminant hepatic failure and is at the highest risk of death without immediate transplantation. He is given a listing designation that supersedes his MELD score. Which of the following best describes this designation?

explanation.summary: Status 1 designation is given to patients in fulminant hepatic failure and supersedes the MELD score.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients can be designated Status 1, usually those in fulminant hepatic failure, and that this designation supersedes the MELD score to prioritize them for a liver.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Extended criteria donor describes a deceased donor with certain risk factors, not a recipient priority listing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PELD score is a numeric urgency score for children under 12, not a designation that overrides MELD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Universal donor refers to a type O blood donor, unrelated to liver listing priority.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A positive lymphocyte cross-match indicates preformed recipient antibodies and does not confer transplant priority.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A transplant surgeon requests a rapid assessment of a donor liver's viability at the time of procurement so that a decision to use the organ can be made quickly. Which of the following is the primary method used to evaluate pre-transplant organs for viability?

explanation.summary: Frozen section evaluation provides the rapid microscopic assessment needed to judge a donor organ's viability at procurement.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that frozen section, in which a portion of tissue is frozen and cut, gives a more immediate microscopic evaluation of pathology, which is what the transplant surgeon needs to quickly decide whether the organ is ready for transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Routine permanent histology gives microscopic detail but takes much longer, so it cannot provide the quick assessment needed at procurement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gross evaluation may be performed but does not provide the microscopic assessment of the degree of pathology.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Electron microscopy is a slow, specialized technique not used for rapid intraoperative viability decisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immunofluorescence is used to detect immune deposits and is not the primary rapid method for donor organ viability.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: During frozen-section evaluation of a potential donor liver, the pathologist reports 65% macrovesicular steatosis. Based on standard criteria described for donor liver assessment, this finding is best interpreted as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acceptable finding with no impact on transplant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Absolute contraindication; the organ will not be used

explanation.summary: Greater than 60% macrovesicular steatosis is an absolute contraindication to using a donor liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that greater than 30% macrovesicular steatosis is a relative contraindication associated with poor early graft function, while greater than 60% macrovesicular steatosis is an absolute contraindication, meaning the organ will not be used. At 65%, this liver crosses the absolute threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Steatosis of this degree is not benign; it strongly predicts poor early graft function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A relative contraindication applies at greater than 30%; at greater than 60% the finding becomes absolute.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rejection is assessed after transplantation, not during pre-transplant donor evaluation, and steatosis is not a rejection finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Steatosis reflects fat accumulation within hepatocytes, not viral infection of the donor liver.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: During frozen-section evaluation of a donor kidney, the pathologist identifies glomeruli showing scarring and hyalinization involving more than half of the glomerular tuft. Which of the following best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Global glomerulosclerosis is scarring or hyalinization of more than half of the glomerulus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines global glomerulosclerosis as scarring/hyalinization of more than half of the glomerulus. It is one of the common donor kidney pathologies assessed on frozen section to determine organ viability.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Arteriolar hyalinization is thickening of arteriole walls by homogenous eosinophilic protein material, not scarring of the glomerulus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interstitial fibrosis affects the interstitium and tubules, not the glomerular tuft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arterial sclerosis is intimal thickening of arteries between the endothelium and internal elastic lamina.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute tubular necrosis involves tubular epithelial injury and is not the glomerular scarring described here.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 years ago remains on lifelong immunosuppressive therapy. He is counseled about the long-term consequences of his medications. Which of the following is the MOST common long-term consequence of his immunosuppressive therapy?

explanation.summary: Long-term immunosuppression most commonly increases the risk of infection, which is more common than malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that transplant patients on long-term immunosuppressive therapy are prone to an increased risk of infection and an increased risk of malignancy, but that infections are much more common than malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased malignancy risk (particularly EBV-related lymphoma) is a real consequence but is less common than infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrence of the primary disease relates to the original disease process rather than to the immunosuppressive therapy itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organ rejection is a risk that is decreased, not increased, by immunosuppressive therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Graft-versus-host disease is not described as a common long-term consequence of solid-organ immunosuppression in this brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplantation

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man undergoes kidney transplantation. Within minutes of vascular anastomosis, the surgeon notes that the graft becomes mottled, cyanotic, and flaccid. Biopsy shows platelet-fibrin thrombi and severe ischemic injury within glomeruli. Which of the following best explains this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pre-formed recipient antibodies against graft endothelial antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ T-cell-mediated destruction of graft parenchymal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation causing vessel occlusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Deposition of IgE antibodies on mast cells

explanation.summary: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours due to pre-formed recipient antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours after transplant when the recipient already has pre-formed antibodies that react against ABO blood group antigens or type I MHC molecules on graft endothelial cells. These antibodies trigger the complement cascade, producing thrombosis, ischemia, and necrosis, which matches the platelet-fibrin thrombi seen on biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ T-cell destruction of graft cells describes acute cellular rejection, which occurs one week to several months later, not within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue describes graft-versus-host disease, seen mainly after bone marrow transplant, not immediate kidney graft failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intimal proliferation and vessel occlusion characterize chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgE on mast cells mediates type I hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, allergy), not antibody-mediated graft thrombosis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man received an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for acute leukemia. Two weeks later he develops a maculopapular skin rash and watery diarrhea. Which of the following cells is most directly responsible for his symptoms?

explanation.summary: GVHD is caused by donor T cells that recognize recipient tissue as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: These symptoms are graft-versus-host disease after bone marrow transplant. Bone marrow transplant tissue contains many T cells, and in GVHD the donor's transplanted T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and attack organs such as the skin and gut, producing rash and diarrhea. GVHD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction mediated by donor T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donor B cells have not been found to cause the symptoms of GVHD; the reaction is T-cell mediated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Recipient T cells drive graft rejection, in which the recipient attacks the graft, the opposite direction of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recipient natural killer cells are not the described mediator of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Donor plasma cells produce antibody; GVHD injury results from donor T-cell cytotoxicity and cytokine release, not humoral immunity.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with diabetic nephropathy receives a kidney transplant. Intraoperatively the surgeon notes the organ is pale and poorly perfused; a thrombus has formed and is preventing perfusion of the graft. Which type of rejection is most likely?

explanation.summary: Rejection occurring within minutes of transplantation is hyperacute.
explanation.whyCorrect: The type of rejection described is hyperacute because it occurred within minutes of transplantation, with thrombosis and poor perfusion caused by pre-formed antibodies activating complement on the graft endothelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute rejection occurs about one week to several months after the transplant, not intraoperatively.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic rejection occurs months to years later and manifests as graft arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Graft-versus-host disease occurs weeks to months after transplant and results mainly from bone marrow transplant, not from an immediate kidney thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subacute rejection is not one of the recognized categories of transplant rejection described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 39-year-old kidney transplant recipient develops rising creatinine 6 weeks after surgery. Biopsy shows inflammatory cells infiltrating between the epithelial cells of the tubules (tubulitis) and CD8+ T cells destroying graft cells. Which of the following best describes this process?

explanation.summary: Tubulitis with CD8+ T-cell-mediated graft cell killing defines acute cellular rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cellular rejection occurs when CD8+ T cells directly destroy graft cells or CD4+ T cells secrete cytokines and induce inflammation. On kidney biopsy it manifests as tubulitis, with inflammatory cells between the epithelial cells of the tubules, matching this patient's findings weeks after transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies binding endothelium with complement activation and shows C4d deposition and capillaritis, not primarily T-cell tubulitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours and shows thrombosis, not a T-cell tubulitis weeks later.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic rejection develops over months to years with graft arteriosclerosis and fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GVHD involves donor T cells attacking recipient tissue and is characteristic of bone marrow, not kidney, transplants.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old kidney transplant recipient has worsening graft function 2 months post-transplant. Biopsy shows peritubular capillaritis, and an immunoperoxidase stain reveals C4d deposition in peritubular capillaries. Which mechanism is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies binding vascular endothelium and activating complement

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE-mediated release of mast cell mediators

choices.label: C
choices.text: Donor T cells attacking recipient endothelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intimal smooth muscle proliferation occluding vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct CD8+ T-cell killing of tubular cells

explanation.summary: C4d deposition marks acute antibody-mediated rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: In acute antibody-mediated rejection, antibodies bind to vascular endothelium and activate complement; the resulting inflammation and endothelial damage cause graft failure. The complement split product C4d deposited in peritubular capillaries, demonstrated by immunoperoxidase staining, is the diagnostic marker.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE and mast cell mediators drive type I hypersensitivity, not complement-fixing antibody rejection of a graft.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Donor T cells attacking the recipient describe GVHD, not antibody-mediated rejection of a kidney graft.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intimal proliferation with vessel occlusion is a feature of chronic rejection, not C4d-positive antibody-mediated injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Direct CD8+ T-cell killing describes acute cellular rejection with tubulitis, which is not marked by C4d deposition.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who received a heart transplant 4 years ago develops progressive graft dysfunction. Angiography shows diffuse narrowing of the coronary arteries, and biopsy reveals graft arteriosclerosis with intimal smooth muscle proliferation. Which type of rejection does this represent?

explanation.summary: Graft arteriosclerosis developing years after transplant is chronic rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic rejection can occur months to years after transplant and involves both cellular and humoral immune responses. It produces graft arteriosclerosis, with intimal smooth muscle proliferation and vessel occlusion, plus interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy, matching the coronary narrowing years after a heart transplant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to 24 hours with thrombosis, not slowly progressive arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute cellular rejection occurs within weeks to months and shows T-cell tubulitis or endothelitis, not chronic arteriosclerosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute antibody-mediated rejection occurs within weeks to months with C4d deposition, not years-long vascular remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GVHD is a bone marrow transplant complication in which donor cells attack the recipient, not chronic coronary graft arteriosclerosis.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops anaphylaxis after a bee sting, with hypotension, urticaria, and bronchospasm. This reaction is mediated by IgE causing release of mast cell mediators. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this, and which type of transplant rejection shares the antibody-mediated category most analogous to hyperacute rejection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type II

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type II hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type I

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type III hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type IV

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type IV hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type III

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type I hypersensitivity; hyperacute rejection is type IV

explanation.summary: Anaphylaxis is type I; hyperacute rejection is a type II (antibody-mediated) reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type I hypersensitivity is immediate, mediated by IgE antibodies that trigger release of mast cell mediators, producing anaphylaxis, allergies, and bronchial asthma. Hyperacute rejection, caused by pre-formed antibodies activating complement against graft endothelium, is classified as a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anaphylaxis is not type II; type II involves IgG/IgM injuring cells, and hyperacute rejection is type II, not type I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaphylaxis is not type III (immune-complex); hyperacute rejection is not type IV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anaphylaxis is not type IV (T-cell mediated); hyperacute rejection is not type III.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anaphylaxis is correctly type I, but hyperacute rejection is type II, not type IV.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man develops an intensely pruritic, vesicular rash 48 hours after his skin contacts poison ivy. Biopsy shows a T-cell-rich infiltrate with macrophage activation and no antibody deposition. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible?

explanation.summary: Contact dermatitis is a delayed, T-cell-mediated type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type IV hypersensitivity reactions occur when T cells cause either direct cytotoxicity (CD8+ T cells) or induce inflammation and cytokine release (CD4+ T cells) with macrophage activation. Examples include contact dermatitis, type I diabetes, and graft-versus-host disease, consistent with this delayed poison ivy reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type I is IgE-mediated and immediate (anaphylaxis, allergy), not a delayed T-cell reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type II involves IgG or IgM injuring cells by phagocytosis or lysis, not T-cell contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type III involves immune-complex deposition (e.g., lupus, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis), not cell-mediated contact dermatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type V is not among the four hypersensitivity categories described in the brick.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A hematologist is counseling a patient before an allogeneic bone marrow transplant about the risk of graft-versus-host disease. Which of the following best explains why GVHD develops in this setting but is rare after solid organ transplants such as kidney?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow transplant tissue contains abundant donor T cells that attack recipient tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: The recipient's pre-formed antibodies react against donor marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recipient CD8+ T cells reject the donor marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complexes deposit in the recipient's bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Donor IgE triggers mast cell degranulation in the recipient

explanation.summary: GVHD occurs because bone marrow grafts are rich in donor T cells that recognize recipient tissue as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bone marrow transplant tissue typically contains a large number of T cells. Unlike graft rejection, in which the recipient's immune cells recognize the graft as foreign, in GVHD the donor's transplanted T cells recognize the recipient's tissues as foreign and attack the recipient's organs, causing severe organ dysfunction. This is why GVHD is characteristic of allogeneic bone marrow, not solid organ, transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pre-formed recipient antibodies against a graft cause hyperacute rejection, not GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recipient CD8+ T cells rejecting the graft describes host-versus-graft rejection, the opposite of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune-complex deposition is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism, not the basis of GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Donor IgE and mast cells describe type I hypersensitivity, which does not mediate GVHD.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with GVHD after bone marrow transplant develops jaundice with a rising direct bilirubin. Which of the following histopathologic changes best accounts for her jaundice?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patchy epithelial cell death in the epidermis

explanation.summary: Jaundice in GVHD results from immune destruction of small bile ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with GVHD may present with jaundice caused by destruction of the small bile ducts, which impairs bile flow and raises bilirubin. This reflects donor T-cell-mediated attack on recipient hepatic tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucosal ulceration of the gut causes the diarrhea of GVHD, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patchy epidermal cell death produces the maculopapular skin rash of GVHD, not jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Graft arteriosclerosis is a feature of chronic solid-organ rejection, not the cause of GVHD-related jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelet-fibrin thrombi characterize hyperacute rejection of a solid organ graft, not GVHD hepatic injury.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is being evaluated for a bone marrow transplant and asks about his risk of graft-versus-host disease. Which of the following is a recognized risk factor for developing GVHD?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young donor age with fully matched HLA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete depletion of donor T cells from the graft

explanation.summary: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients exposed to radiation or with leukemia, autoimmune disease, or immunodeficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: GVHD occurs most frequently in recipients who have been exposed to radiation or who have leukemia, autoimmune diseases, or immunodeficiencies. Other contributing factors include transplantation from female donors to male recipients. Some of this risk relates to immunosuppression of the recipient, reducing the ability to neutralize the donor T-lymphocyte attack.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A young, fully HLA-matched donor reduces rather than increases the alloreactivity that drives GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recipients are typically conditioned with chemotherapy to eradicate marrow; absence of chemotherapy is not a listed GVHD risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GVHD requires an allogeneic (non-identical donor) graft; autologous transplants use the patient's own cells and do not cause GVHD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Depleting donor T cells removes the very cells that mediate GVHD, lowering the risk.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A transplant team manages a kidney recipient on multiple immunosuppressive drugs. The team notes that standardized histologic criteria are used to diagnose and grade rejection across organs. Which criteria are used specifically for grading rejection in kidney transplants?

explanation.summary: The Banff criteria are used to grade kidney transplant rejection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several histologic criteria have been created to diagnose and grade rejection for organ transplants. The Banff criteria are used for kidney transplants, while the ISHLT criteria are applied to heart transplants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ISHLT criteria are used for heart transplant rejection, not kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ranson criteria assess the severity of acute pancreatitis, not transplant rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Child-Pugh criteria grade chronic liver disease severity, not graft rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNM staging describes cancer extent, not transplant rejection grading.

questions.topicName: Diseases of the Immune System: Transplant Rejection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has long-standing abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss. Endoscopic biopsies are obtained. A duodenal biopsy shows a normal villous height-to-crypt ratio of 3:1. A biopsy of the sigmoid colon shows collections of neutrophils within colonic crypts and a nodular aggregation of histiocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A nodular aggregate of histiocytes (non-caseating granuloma) in the bowel wall is the classic clue for Crohn's disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that classically features nodular aggregates of histiocytes, i.e., non-caseating granulomas, and can affect any segment of the GI tract. The normal duodenal villous architecture argues against a malabsorptive enteropathy and points to a transmural granulomatous IBD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Campylobacter jejuni causes an acute invasive enterocolitis but does not produce granulomatous inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Celiac disease produces duodenal villous atrophy with a reduced villous-to-crypt ratio; here the ratio is a normal 3:1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clostridioides difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis without granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative colitis characteristically lacks granulomas and is limited to continuous mucosal disease of the colon and rectum.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops migratory joint pain, red and light-sensitive eyes, and painful urination about two weeks after an episode of bloody diarrhea. Which of the following pathogens was most likely responsible for her preceding gastrointestinal illness?

explanation.summary: Reactive arthritis (arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis) after diarrhea is a classic sequela of Campylobacter jejuni.
explanation.whyCorrect: Campylobacter jejuni infection is an important trigger of reactive arthritis, an immune-mediated triad of joint pain, conjunctivitis (light sensitivity), and urethritis (painful urination) that follows the enteric infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytomegalovirus can involve the eye and GI tract in immunocompromised hosts, but post-infectious reactive arthritis would be highly unusual.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Escherichia coli O157:H7 causes bloody diarrhea and may trigger hemolytic uremic syndrome, not reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giardia lamblia causes malabsorption with greasy stools and is not associated with reactive arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Herpes simplex virus can cause mucosal ulceration but does not classically produce reactive arthritis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has several months of bloody diarrhea and tenesmus. Colonoscopy shows continuous mucosal inflammation extending proximally from the rectum without intervening areas of normal mucosa. Biopsies show crypt abscesses limited to the mucosa and superficial submucosa, without granulomas. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Continuous colonic inflammation limited to the mucosa/superficial submucosa without granulomas is ulcerative colitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum and shows continuous involvement of the mucosa and superficial submucosa, typically with crypt abscesses and without granulomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Celiac disease affects the small bowel with villous atrophy, not the colon with continuous mucosal colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Crohn's disease produces skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and non-caseating granulomas rather than continuous superficial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CMV colitis occurs in immunocompromised patients and shows owl's eye viral inclusions, not this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giardiasis is a small-bowel protozoal infection causing malabsorption, not a chronic continuous colitis.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, bloating, and iron-deficiency anemia that improve when she removes wheat, barley, and rye from her diet. Duodenal biopsy shows flattened villi with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. Which of the following best explains the intestinal injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An immune response to gliadin, a component of gluten

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial invasion of the colonic mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Owl's eye viral inclusions in endothelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protozoal colonization of the small-bowel lumen

explanation.summary: Celiac disease results from an immune response to gliadin (a gluten protein) that damages the duodenal mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Celiac disease results from intestinal inflammation triggered by an immune response to gliadin, a constituent of the grain protein gluten, producing tissue damage and duodenal villous atrophy; symptoms resolve with gluten avoidance.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial mucosal invasion describes infectious colitis, not the gluten-driven small-bowel enteropathy shown here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomatous inflammation is characteristic of Crohn's disease, not celiac disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Owl's eye inclusions are seen in cytomegalovirus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Luminal protozoal colonization describes giardiasis, which does not cause immune villous atrophy responsive to gluten withdrawal.

questions.topicName: Immune-related and Infectious Causes of Diarrhea

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with biopsy-proven celiac disease develops an intensely itchy, grouped vesicular rash over the extensor surfaces of his elbows and knees.
